scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Circle of Sardinia
This is Ballu tundu. 19th century.
on_screen: Title card: Ballu tundu · Italy · 19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is believed to derive from prehistoric sacred ceremonies.
It has been documented since the early 19th century, with oral transmission ensuring its survival through generations.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It serves as a communal expression of social aggregation, historically linked to propitiating harvests or hunting success.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form a circle, holding hands or arms.
The movement involves a rhythmic, pulsing motion of the trunk, while the legs execute precise steps.
The circle rotates clockwise.
Watch for Sa seria, Su sartiu.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Clockwise rotation in a circle.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Traditional instruments include the launeddas, organetto diatonico, accordion, harmonica, and various reed flutes.
Vocal accompaniment, such as the 'canto a tenore', is also common.
Listen for the launeddas, accordion, organetto diatonico, harmonica.
The pulse is 6/8.
The music is characterized by a rhythmic pulse that drives the dancers, often featuring the unique drone and melodic interplay of the launeddas or the energetic bellows of the accordion.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Passus de Ballu — Ireneo Massidda

scenes.title: The people
narration: Includes musicians like Efisio Melis (launeddas), Francesco Bande (accordion), and Antonio Masala (accordion).
Variants include 'su ballu antigu', 'su ballu seriu', 'su passu torrau', and 'su ballu e Ulassa', which differ in tempo and structure.
Part of the broader family of Sardinian folk dances (balli sardi), with connections to both monostructured and bistructured rhythmic patterns.
